The Bourke's parrot (Neopsephotus bourkii) is a small, sexually dimorphic psittaculid endemic to the arid and semi-arid interior of Australia. Hatchlings emerge from the incubated egg weighing just 3.75 grams [Ww0 = 3.75 grams], a figure that reflects the altricial condition typical of the order Psittaciformes. Egg development proceeds over an incubation period of approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days] at a nest temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a value consistent with the thermal regime reported for other cavity-nesting parrots of similar body size. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning, with the initial wet weight representing the total mass of the newly emerged chick after yolk absorption. This low initial mass is comparatively modest among Australian parrots, yet it appears sufficient to fuel the rapid developmental trajectory that culminates in first feeding and the early nestling period. Field observations of nests in the Mulga woodlands of Western Australia have confirmed these basic life-history parameters, which are essential for constructing accurate population models for this species.

During the nestling phase, the downy chick grows rapidly under the biparental care typical of the species. At the resting body temperature characteristic of an active, normothermic bird of approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], fledging—the point at which the young bird achieves its first flight and departs the nest—occurs at 27 days after hatching [tx = 27 days after hatching]. This fledgling age is relatively short for a parrot of its ultimate adult body size, likely an adaptation to the unpredictable rainfall and food availability of its xeric habitat. Sexual maturity, defined as the attainment of puberty and the onset of gonadal maturation, follows a different developmental schedule. At the same baseline thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], individuals reach puberty approximately 90 days after hatching [tp = approximately 90 days after hatching]. This extended period between fledging and reproductive activation likely reflects the time required for a young bird to acquire sufficient foraging experience and build the somatic reserves necessary for the energetic demands of courtship and nesting in a challenging environment.

Reproductive investment in the Bourke's parrot is constrained by the brevity of the austral spring and the erratic availability of seeding grasses. Breeding females produce approximately 4 to 5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 to 5 clutches per year], with each clutch containing 1 egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing 1 egg], a modest fecundity for an arid-zone species. The first successful breeding event typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals delay first reproduction until their second calendar year, taking advantage of the seasonal rains that follow their birth year at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This deferred first reproduction is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survivorship in a variable environment. The ultimate adult body mass also reflects this slow pace: females attain an asymptotic mass of 40.1 grams [Wwi = 40.1 grams], while the slightly larger males reach 42.7 grams [Wwi = 42.7 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism that is often correlated with male competition for nest hollows.

Energetic expenditure in this species is dominated by the high costs of thermoregulation and flight. Basal metabolic rate, measured under standard respirometry conditions in post-absorptive, resting birds at thermoneutrality, reaches 97 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 97 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This BMR value is relatively elevated for a small avian granivore and likely reflects the high surface-area-to-volume ratio that necessitates substantial metabolic heat production to maintain core temperature during the cold desert nights. The maximum longevity of the Bourke's parrot, based on the oldest known wild individual, is approximately 19.4 years [am = approximately 19.4 years] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This considerable lifespan, which far exceeds that of many similar-sized passerines, is a hallmark of the general psittaciform life-history syndrome of low annual fecundity coupled with high adult survival. The combination of a high BMR with an extended lifespan is somewhat counterintuitive from a simple metabolic-rate-longevity perspective but is consistent with the cognitive and social complexity that characterizes parrots.

The life-history profile of Neopsephotus bourkii can be situated within a broader comparative context among Australian arid-zone parrots. The combination of a 3.75 gram [Ww0 = 3.75 gram] hatchling mass that develops into an adult female weighing 40.1 grams [Wwi = 40.1 grams] and an adult male weighing 42.7 grams [Wwi = 42.7 grams] represents a considerable postnatal growth increment. The timing of key developmental milestones—incubation to hatching at a nest temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] over 18 days [ab = 18 days], fledging at 27 days after hatching [tx = 27 days after hatching], and the attainment of puberty at 90 days after hatching [tp = 90 days after hatching], the latter two both recorded at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]—defines a compressed juvenile period relative to the lengthy lifespan. The first reproduction at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] and the annual production of approximately 4 to 5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 to 5 clutches per year] of 1 egg each [N_R_i = 1 egg each] underscore a bet-hedging reproductive strategy adapted to erratic resource pulses at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The basal metabolic rate of 97 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 97 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] and the maximum lifespan of 19.4 years [am = 19.4 years] together paint a picture of a species that, while energetically expensive to maintain, has evolved a remarkably durable life-history design suited to the challenges of life in the Australian outback.
